The passage discusses Lin Zexu’s complaint about the opium trade imposed by foreigners (mainly the British) on China.  
He points out that Britain prohibits opium at home but exports it to China, harming its people.  
Historically, the British began large-scale opium exports to China to offset a trade imbalance caused by high British demand for Chinese goods (especially tea and silk), for which they had to pay in silver.  
Because China was largely self-sufficient and had little demand for European goods, the British used opium—produced in their colony India—to create a new commodity demand in China and reverse the silver drain.  

The key background fact driving European (British) actions was China’s restrictive trade system, which limited European sales in China, leading to the opium trade as a solution.
